newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine farmers want sugar rebate withdrawn.
newsitem.headline: Philippine farmers want sugar rebate withdrawn.

text.p: Philippine sugar farmers and millers asked the government on Tuesday to suspend immediately the 35 percent tariff rebate on refined sugar imports from neighbouring countries to protect the local industry.

"If nothing changes in the rules beginning July 1, most sugar producers will be on the verge of bankruptcy," Governor Rafael Coscolluela of Negros in Visayas island, the country's main sugar producing province, told a news conference.
Under present rules, the Philippines gives a 35 percent tariff discount on refined sugar imports from member-nations of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
By July 1 this year, the tariff on refined sugar imported by the Philippines from other ASEAN countries is expected to drop from the present 65 percent to 52.5 percent.

The tariff on Philippine sugar imports from non-ASEAN countries is also scheduled to drop from 100 percent to 80 percent by July 1 as part of the country's commitment to the World Trade Organisation, Coscoluella said.

Agriculture Secretary Salvador Escudero said last month he had asked the Tariff Commission to raise the tariff on imported sugar to 133 percent from 100 percent from January 1 to June 30, 1997, and to 100 percent from 80 percent from July 1 to August 31.
The Philippine Tariff Commission has yet to act on Escudero's request.

Philippine Sugar Millers Association (PSMA) executive director Jose Maria Zabaleta said the Philippines was the only sugar producer and importer among Southeast Asian countries that gave a tariff rebate on sugar.
Coscolluela blamed the drop in the prices of local raw sugars to the importation of cheaper refined sugar from neighbouring countries in the past several months.

With a 52.5 percent tariff on refined sugar from Southeast Asian nations by July this year, the equivalent raw value of imported sugar is only 508 pesos per 50-kg bag compared to the local farm gate price of 530 pesos per bag for locally produced sugar, he said.
Local planters and millers pegged their costs in producing sugar at 627 pesos per bag, higher than the 488 pesos per bag estimate of the state Sugar Regulatory Administration (SRA), said Coscolluela.
Domestic raw sugar prices were pegged at 750 to 800 pesos per bag at the start of 1996.

Coscolluela said the drop in local raw prices was hurting small farmers. There are 370,000 hectares of sugar lands in the country cultivated by 100,000 planters. Farmers cultivating 10 hectares and below comprise 81 percent of the sugar lands, according to data from the PSMA.
Coscolluela said one hectare of sugar land in Negros yielded at most 60 bags (at 50 kg each) of raw sugar each crop year.
The Department of Trade and Industry said in a previous report the Philippines imported $60 million worth of refined sugar, mostly from Thailand, from January to September 1996.
It said the country's imports from Southeast Asian nations reached $44 million in the period. "More than 90 percent of our sugar imports from ASEAN comes from Thailand," it said.
SRA administrator Wilson Gamboa has said that import of some 1.2 million tonnes between September 1995 and July 1996, led to a glut in the local market.
